title: Why I Changed My Mind About the Death Penalty
text:
We had to crawl . We were warned not to lift our faces. We had to press our noses to the floor. The hotel was cheap and the carpet stank. The TV was on but we did not hear it, because we were listening for commands. There was a man standing over us while we crawled. He was telling us where to go. He was ordering us to crawl to the bathtub, and he had a gun, a very big one, the single legible shadow in a situation of enforced blindness.

 The bathtub was a surprise, the second in a series. The first was his presence in the room. We were salesmen, on the road. It was night, and I had gone to my colleague Steven’s room to drink whiskey and smoke pot and watch television. I had made a mistake and left the door to the room ajar, and while I was taking a piss, a gun barrel nipped the flesh of my temple and turned my head at an angle from my shoulders. I was marched like that, like a marionette, back into the room, where Steven was sitting on the bed with his back propped against the headboard. He tried to move backwards, as if pedaling on a bicycle, but the headboard stopped him. His expression changed five times until it settled into a kind of antic sadness, like the mask of tragedy.

 The man with the gun—the robber, the thief, the gunman, the intruder, I still don’t know what to call him—made us lie on the bed, our faces in the pillows. He stayed a long time, asking us questions and letting us know that lies would carry mortal consequence. He thought we were hiding money. “You’re not lying to me, are you? You better not be.” For a while, we passed the test. Then something changed, and he told us to get on the floor and crawl.

 The bathtub was small and cold and hard to climb into from our prostration on the bathroom floor, especially with someone assuring us that he would kill us if we looked at his face. How could we not look at his face? I looked at his face when I looked at the gun. He had a dapper pointed mustache and he was sweating profusely and the round hole at the end of the long barrel was somehow blacker than the gun itself, somehow more absolute. “I told you not to look at me,” he said, and it was the reasonableness of his voice that made everything speed up, that made me want to cling to every passing moment.

 He told Steven to turn the tap and run the water and Steven, instead, folded his hands before him and said, “Oh, Jesus Christ, please don’t kill us.” The man behind the gun responded with seeming annoyance: “Don’t ‘Jesus’ me. I’m a God-fearing motherfucker myself.” I worried that the annoyance would be fatal but when I looked at him again, the gun was no longer the empty eye staring at my head. He lifted the barrel, told us not to call the cops for another 15 minutes, and left.

 We did not wait 15 minutes. The cops came, and treated it, at first, as just another hotel-room holdup. But one detail mystified the lead investigator. He had been to many crime scenes in his life, but usually when people were forced into a bathtub at gunpoint they did not get out. “What happened to them?” I asked, for I was 22 years old, until that moment still a boy.

 “They were executed,” he said. “Putting you in the bathtub is an execution scenario.”

 An execution scenario—so that was it. That was what had happened. I couldn’t quite bring myself to say it, but once the word execution spelled itself out in my brain, it stayed there, a tightly knotted cord, a hangman’s noose, forever. I, along with Steven, had been put through the paces of execution. I had survived being put through the paces of execution.

 [ Elizabeth Bruenig: The woman who has prevented 200 executions ] 

 When a detective called two months later with the news that the man who robbed us had been arrested, the first question I asked was “Did he kill anyone?” The detective demurred; he said, “You don’t have to worry about that,” because the sweaty gunman with the dapper mustache had robbed so many salesmen in so many marginal hotels that he didn’t need to bring me in to testify. I never got the answer to my question. Nor did I think to get the man’s name. But there existed for many years an alternative version of events in which he did kill someone, in which Steven didn’t invoke the Lord’s name and I wound up as splash and splatter in a hotel bathtub.

 I was fired from my sales job shortly after the detective’s call. I began writing, and the first thing I wrote about was what had happened in the hotel room, and what I’d had to surrender, in terms of will. I also began thinking about the other kind of execution, the state-sanctioned practice we call the death penalty. I made a decision about it, and the decision surprised me.

 I had grown up Catholic, at a time when the pro-life Church placed nearly as much emphasis on opposing the death penalty and euthanasia as it did on abortion. But I approved of the death penalty. I couldn’t call myself an advocate, or even a proponent. I just believed in the essential rightness of it, because I knew that life or death is a decision—because I knew, with the certainty of experience, that the man who’d exiled me to a bathtub and pointed a gun at my head had not only the power of life and death, but the power of choice. He was not in a rush, he was not making his getaway, he was not panicking, he didn’t seem at all afraid. He had held us captive for nearly 45 minutes, and then he decided whether to kill us or let us live.

 It was my memory of his deliberation, the icy luxury of time on his hands, that formed the rationale for my belief that the death penalty was not murder, but a necessary answer to murder. Had he taken our lives, he would have chosen to deny us mercy—and so to him mercy must be denied. I didn’t believe in the efficacy of the death penalty as a deterrent. I believed that anyone who decides to kill has also decided to be killed. I believed that murder is an eternal crime that must be punished in kind.

 I was not proud of this belief, but I held on to it as it held on to me. I kept it in some secret stash of my soul when I wrote, back in the ’90s, about a jailbird hipster who had been sentenced to death for murdering a Domino’s employee named John Collins. I’d gotten to know Tony Mobley. In the course of interviewing him, I asked him what it was like to kill a man. He made it sound like a rare thrill. He also showed me the word DOMINO proudly tattooed on his shoulder, a mark that carried the force of a biblical stain.

 I was grateful to him for his honesty, and that made it awkward to admit to myself—though never to him—that I thought the jury had ultimately made the right call. But 10 years after I met him, I still went down to the big state penitentiary south of Atlanta and kept vigil just outside the gates on the night he was supposed to die.

 I did not go as a reporter. I drove to the prison on a whim, a sudden pang of guilt and curiosity and obligation, the first and only time I put myself in the vicinity of a government execution. It was cloudy and cold and damp, a night of continual shivers. There were a few people on hand, most of them members of a death-row ministry, praying. I didn’t know if anyone was inside, for Tony. I knew that members of the Collins family had declined to attend; they had asked the state to spare the man who’d killed John—because killing Tony wouldn’t bring him back. I drank coffee to keep warm and I waited. But for what? I had always viewed the death penalty from the perspective of my own crouching helplessness in the bathtub, the endless instants that passed with my life in another’s hands. Now I was waiting outside a prison where, somewhere inside, a person I knew was being strapped down and killed. I was waiting for news that the killing had been successful, and I was drinking coffee.

 Tony Mobley died at 8 p.m. on March 1, 2005. He had withheld mercy from John Collins and mercy had been withheld from him. And yet when the prison spokesman emerged from behind the gates to say that the sentence had been carried out and justice had been done, I did not feel that something had been set aright, that the scales had been balanced. I began asking a question so obvious, it embarrassed me. If my experience on my knees in a bathtub told me that the great sin of murder was not just the taking of a life but the cold, rational, deliberative process that led to it, how was what had just happened anything less than murderous? The death penalty is not an impersonal manifestation of karmic justice; it must be “administered” by fallible human beings working for an even more fallible system that labors under the pretense of blind and impartial judgment. What gives us the right? What gives anyone the right? As much as part of my soul cried out for the satisfaction of the death penalty, the answer that came to me is that we don’t have the right.

 We do not live in a pro-life country, and I am aware that for some readers, my argument against the death penalty for a murderer with DOMINO printed on his shoulder will sound less convincing than my argument for it. We do not, as a people, like to look at how we kill our killers. We especially don’t like to face up to the racial disparities of death row and the growing body of evidence suggesting that the innocent have died along with the guilty. But every so often we have the chance to see how very personal the impersonal machinations of capital punishment really are, with the lies and the pieties stripped away.

 This happened recently, when Christa Pike, paying for her part in the torture and murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, went into the death chamber in Tennessee, and somehow came out alive. She was put through the paces of execution, but the drugs injected into her arm while she was strapped to the gurney failed to kill her, and so, as the state of Tennessee sought to answer murder with murder, it wound up answering torture with torture . As of this writing, we don’t know if it will try to kill her again, but that haze of indecision did not stop Senator Marsha Blackburn from using her successful run for governor to declare that what Pike’s failed execution really proves is that we ought to “bring back the electric chair.” Torture, then, is not enough; we have to smell the burning scalp.

 Nobody likes to think of themselves as bloodthirsty. I certainly did not like to think of myself as bloodthirsty when I supported the death penalty, only as realistic, rational, and in favor of cosmic reckonings. But, around the same time Pike lived to die another day, “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth did us the favor of being openly bloodthirsty, and counting on the rest of America to be equally forthright. He came up with the idea that if what the mass murderer Nidal Hasan needed was execution by military firing squad, then what America needed was to watch it , “on streaming.” He sought to shore up our flagging national resolve, but his actual achievement was to elicit what has been so hard to come by for the past 10 years: our shame.

 [ Elizabeth Bruenig: Public execution won’t have the effect Trump intends ] 

 Is shame the right word for what subsequently compelled Governor Gavin Newsom to commute the sentences of all 548 prisoners on California’s death row? It isn’t, although Newsom reportedly saw the Christa Pike debacle as an opportunity to press forward with a moral argument that, of necessity, will become a political one. He wrote, in his letter announcing the decision , that “state-sanctioned killing” is something that “diminishes each of us.” It is a powerful letter, confident in its sweep: “Many Californians feel that those who commit brutal crimes deserve to die. But as governor, I have concluded the state cannot morally kill them.”

 The absolutism of that last sentence made me think of the bathtub, and the beliefs that followed me out of it. Am I ashamed of the conviction that resulted from coming face-to-face with a shiny black .45, which spoke of nothing more eloquently than my own death? I am not, in part because if I am honest with myself, I have to say that I have no idea what shape my convictions would take if a member of my family died in an “execution scenario” or, for that matter, in a random act of violence. All I know is this: I survived. And I survived because I was spared. Was I spared because, as the cop on the scene suggested, my colleague Steven called upon Jesus Christ? I can’t say I wasn’t, but at the same time, my continued presence on this Earth was not and is not a miracle. I was spared because a human being spared me.

 [ From the December 2019 issue: Tom Junod on Mister Rogers’s enduring wisdom ] 

 I will never know the name of the man who made me crawl, fire having consumed his police file long ago, and I don’t like to give him too much credit, in case he did execute someone else. But I had gotten the story wrong, and it led me for a time to the wrong conclusions. I always contended that had he killed me, he should in turn be killed, if only to demonstrate what my life was worth. But in fact he didn’t kill me. He had power over me—an absolute power I can’t contemplate without getting a little sick—and he lifted his gun.

 I will never know why. I can only state a truth still hard to say, because it obliges me to him. He terrorized me, and he took something from me, not only money. But my life began when he gave me something back. It is hard to think of a guy pointing a gun at your head as merciful, especially now, decades later, when mercy is in such short supply. But I am here both despite and because of him. I am here because he, a criminal, a villain, a robber, and possibly a murderer, was able to give me, in a moment of the most extreme exigency, something that is beyond so many death-state governors and Supreme Court justices deliberating matters of life and death at their leisure.

 I have marked the beginning of my life from the moment of my survival. I have lived more than 40 years past the bathtub. But I was, and remain, a child of mercy, old enough now to know that there are bathtubs everywhere, and mercy is all we’ve got.

 This article appears in the January 2027 print edition with the headline “An Execution Scenario.”
